overview: The SQL BETWEEN operator filters rows where a column value falls within a specified range, replacing a pair of comparison conditions with a single, readable expression.
BETWEEN is inclusive on BOTH bounds: `col BETWEEN a AND b` is exactly equivalent to `col >= a AND col <= b`.
It works on numbers, dates/timestamps, and even strings (using collation order), and pairs with NOT (`NOT BETWEEN`) to select values outside the range.
learningObjectives: Understand that BETWEEN is inclusive on both the lower and upper bounds and is shorthand for >= AND <=.
Apply BETWEEN to numeric and date/timestamp ranges, and use NOT BETWEEN to exclude ranges.
Avoid the classic date-boundary and off-by-one pitfalls that silently drop or include rows.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: BETWEEN is a SQL range predicate of the form `expr BETWEEN low AND high`, which evaluates to TRUE when `expr >= low AND expr <= high`. Both endpoints are included in the result set. The predicate returns NULL (treated as not-true, so the row is excluded) if any of expr, low, or high is NULL. NOT BETWEEN negates the predicate, returning TRUE when the value is strictly below low or strictly above high.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: BETWEEN is like asking 'is this number inside this range, including the edges?' If you ask for ages BETWEEN 18 AND 65, someone who is exactly 18 and someone who is exactly 65 both qualify. It's just a shorter, clearer way of writing 'greater-than-or-equal to 18 AND less-than-or-equal to 65'.
coreConcept.historicalContext: BETWEEN has been part of the SQL standard since SQL-86 and is supported by virtually every relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite). It was introduced as syntactic sugar to make range filters more declarative and readable than chained comparison operators, and its inclusive semantics were standardized to remove ambiguity across vendors.

whyItMatters.business: Range filtering underlies nearly every report: sales in a date window, customers in an age bracket, transactions in a price tier. Correct inclusive bounds mean financial and operational reports count the right records, avoiding under- or over-reporting that misleads decisions.
whyItMatters.engineering: BETWEEN expresses intent clearly and compactly, reducing copy-paste errors from repeating a column name in two comparisons. It is fully sargable, so the optimizer can use B-tree indexes for efficient range scans.
whyItMatters.scalability: On large tables, a BETWEEN on an indexed column lets the engine perform an index range scan instead of a full table scan, dramatically reducing I/O as data volume grows.
whyItMatters.cost: Efficient range scans read fewer pages, lowering CPU and I/O — directly reducing compute cost in cloud warehouses billed per byte scanned or per query.
whyItMatters.reliability: Predictable inclusive semantics make queries deterministic and easy to reason about, reducing the risk of subtle data-correctness bugs in production pipelines.

coreComponents.name: Test Expression (expr)
coreComponents.definition: The column or expression whose value is checked against the range.
coreComponents.purpose: Provides the value being filtered, e.g. a price, age, or order_date.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be type-comparable with both bounds; should ideally be an indexed column for performance.

coreComponents.name: Lower Bound (low)
coreComponents.definition: The inclusive minimum value of the range, written before AND.
coreComponents.purpose: Sets the smallest value that qualifies; values equal to low are included.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be less than or equal to the upper bound, otherwise the predicate matches nothing.

coreComponents.name: Upper Bound (high)
coreComponents.definition: The inclusive maximum value of the range, written after AND.
coreComponents.purpose: Sets the largest value that qualifies; values equal to high are included.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be greater than or equal to the lower bound; for timestamps, be careful that midnight excludes the rest of the last day.

internalWorking: The SQL parser rewrites `expr BETWEEN low AND high` internally into the equivalent `expr >= low AND expr <= high` before optimization.
The query optimizer evaluates whether the test expression is on an indexed column; if so, it can plan a B-tree index range scan, seeking to `low` and scanning forward until it passes `high`.
If any operand is NULL, three-valued logic yields UNKNOWN for the predicate, so the row is not returned (the same behavior as the expanded >= AND <= form).
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Query Parser (BETWEEN -> >= AND <=) -> Optimizer (chooses index range scan vs. full scan) -> Storage Engine (reads qualifying pages) -> Result Set (inclusive of both bounds)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A user submits `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 500;`.
2. The parser expands this to `amount >= 100 AND amount <= 500`.
3. The optimizer sees an index on `amount` and selects an index range scan from 100 up to 500 inclusive.
4. The storage engine returns every row whose amount is 100, 500, or anything in between; rows with amount = 99.99 or 500.01 are excluded.

keyTerminology.meaning: Both the lower and upper endpoints are part of the matched range.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines the exact semantics of BETWEEN; misremembering it as exclusive causes off-by-one errors.

keyTerminology.meaning: A predicate (Search ARGument ABLE) that the optimizer can satisfy with an index seek/range scan rather than a full scan.
keyTerminology.importance: BETWEEN on a bare indexed column is sargable, which is why it is preferred over wrapping the column in a function.

keyTerminology.meaning: A range that includes the lower bound but excludes the upper, written as `>= a AND < b`.
keyTerminology.importance: The recommended pattern for timestamp ranges to avoid the midnight-boundary pitfall that BETWEEN introduces.

importantConcepts.explanation: `ts BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` compares a TIMESTAMP against dates interpreted as midnight (00:00:00). Any event on 2024-01-31 after midnight (e.g. 2024-01-31 09:15) is EXCLUDED because it is greater than '2024-01-31 00:00:00'. Prefer `ts >= '2024-01-01' AND ts < '2024-02-01'`.
`BETWEEN high AND low` (e.g. `BETWEEN 500 AND 100`) does NOT auto-swap the values; it expands to `>= 500 AND <= 100`, which is impossible, so it returns zero rows. The lower value must come first.

variationsAndTypes: **Numeric BETWEEN:** Filters integers or decimals within an inclusive range, e.g. `salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000`.
**Date/Timestamp BETWEEN:** Filters temporal values; safe for pure DATE columns but risky for TIMESTAMP columns due to the midnight boundary.
**NOT BETWEEN:** Returns rows strictly outside the range, equivalent to `expr < low OR expr > high`.
**String BETWEEN:** Less common; compares text using the column's collation, e.g. `name BETWEEN 'A' AND 'M'` selects names whose collation order falls in that span.
advantages: **Readability:** A single, declarative expression replaces two comparisons and avoids repeating the column name.
**Inclusive clarity:** Standardized inclusive-on-both-ends semantics are consistent across all major databases.
**Sargable performance:** Works with B-tree indexes for efficient range scans on large tables.
**NOT support:** NOT BETWEEN cleanly expresses 'outside this range' without manual OR logic.
disadvantages: **Timestamp footgun:** The inclusive upper bound combined with implicit midnight conversion silently drops most of the last day.
**No auto-swap:** Reversed bounds yield no rows instead of an error, making mistakes hard to notice.
**NULL handling surprises:** A NULL bound or value silently excludes rows, which can mask data issues.
**Less explicit for half-open ranges:** Modern best practice for time windows favors `>= AND <`, which BETWEEN cannot express.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use BETWEEN for inclusive numeric ranges, age/price brackets, and pure DATE-column windows where both endpoints genuinely belong to the result, and when readability of an inclusive range is the goal.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid BETWEEN for TIMESTAMP/DATETIME windows (use `>= start AND < end` instead) and whenever the upper bound should be exclusive, to prevent silently dropping or double-counting boundary rows.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: BETWEEN is like a museum admission sign that says 'free entry for ages 5 to 12'. A child who just turned 5 and a child who is exactly 12 both get in free — the edges count. If the sign instead meant 'up to but not including 12', a 12-year-old would have to pay, which is the difference between inclusive (BETWEEN) and an exclusive upper bound.

commonMisconceptions.myth: BETWEEN excludes one or both of the endpoints.
commonMisconceptions.reality: BETWEEN is inclusive on BOTH ends. `x BETWEEN 1 AND 10` includes both 1 and 10. There is no version of standard BETWEEN that is exclusive.
They are identical to the optimizer — the parser rewrites BETWEEN into exactly that pair of comparisons, so performance is the same.

productionConsiderations.scalability: On large fact tables, BETWEEN on an indexed (or partitioned) date column enables index range scans and partition pruning, keeping query cost proportional to the range size rather than the whole table.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Standardized inclusive semantics make BETWEEN deterministic across environments; the main reliability risk is timestamp boundaries, which should be handled with half-open ranges.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: BETWEEN itself is stateless; correctness depends on consistent data types between the column and bounds, so enforce explicit casts to avoid implicit-conversion surprises after schema changes.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch for reports whose row counts jump at month/day boundaries — a classic symptom of the BETWEEN timestamp trap. Compare counts against half-open-range equivalents.
productionConsiderations.security: Always parameterize bound values rather than concatenating user input into the SQL string to prevent SQL injection in range filters.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: In pay-per-scan warehouses, pairing BETWEEN with partitioned date columns prunes partitions and minimizes bytes scanned, directly lowering query cost.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep the test expression as a bare indexed column; wrapping it in a function (e.g. `DATE(ts) BETWEEN ...`) makes the predicate non-sargable and forces a full scan.

codeExamples.title: Numeric and NOT BETWEEN range filtering
codeExamples.overview: Selects orders within a price band using inclusive BETWEEN, then shows the exact >= AND <= equivalent and NOT BETWEEN for values outside the band.
codeExamples.code:
-- Inclusive: includes amount = 100 and amount = 500
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 500;

-- Exactly equivalent expanded form
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE amount >= 100 AND amount <= 500;

-- Everything outside the band (amount < 100 OR amount > 500)
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE amount NOT BETWEEN 100 AND 500;
codeExamples.breakdown: The first query returns rows with amount in [100, 500], endpoints included. The second proves the equivalence the parser uses internally. The third, NOT BETWEEN, returns rows strictly below 100 or strictly above 500 — boundary values 100 and 500 are NOT returned by it.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: BETWEEN returns rows with amount of exactly 100, exactly 500, and all values in between. NOT BETWEEN returns the complementary set (amount < 100 or > 500), excluding 100 and 500.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Writing `BETWEEN 500 AND 100` (bounds reversed) returns zero rows because it expands to `>= 500 AND <= 100`. NULL amounts are excluded by both BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Ensure an index exists on `amount` so the optimizer performs a range scan instead of a full table scan.

codeExamples.title: The date-boundary pitfall and the safe half-open fix
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates how BETWEEN on a TIMESTAMP column silently drops same-day events and the recommended half-open `>= AND <` pattern.
codeExamples.code:
-- RISKY: created_at is a TIMESTAMP. '2024-01-31' is read as 2024-01-31 00:00:00,
-- so an order at 2024-01-31 14:30 is EXCLUDED.
SELECT order_id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31';

-- SAFE: half-open interval captures the entire month, all timestamps included
SELECT order_id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2024-02-01';

-- Pure DATE column: BETWEEN is safe because there is no time component
SELECT order_id, order_day
FROM orders
WHERE order_day BETWEEN DATE '2024-01-01' AND DATE '2024-01-31';
codeExamples.breakdown: With a TIMESTAMP column, the upper bound '2024-01-31' becomes midnight, so anything later that day fails `<= 2024-01-31 00:00:00`. The half-open form `>= start AND < next_period_start` includes every instant of January regardless of time. For a true DATE column there is no time-of-day, so BETWEEN is correct.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The risky query under-counts January by omitting all Jan 31 events after midnight. The safe query returns the full month. The DATE-column query also returns the full month correctly.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming a date literal carries an end-of-day time; mixing DATE and TIMESTAMP types causing implicit conversions; using `<= '2024-01-31 23:59:59'` which still misses sub-second events in the final second.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer the half-open `>= AND <` pattern universally for time windows; it keeps the predicate sargable and works on both DATE and TIMESTAMP columns without time-of-day surprises.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail analytics team needs a daily revenue report for the month of January 2024. Their initial query uses BETWEEN on a TIMESTAMP order column and the totals look slightly low; they must produce a correct, defensible monthly figure.
endToEndExample.inputData: An `orders` table with columns order_id (INT), customer_id (INT), amount (DECIMAL), and created_at (TIMESTAMP). Orders span late December 2023 through early February 2024, with many orders on January 31 at various times of day.
endToEndExample.architecture: A PostgreSQL OLTP database with a B-tree index on created_at. The report query runs from a BI tool that parameterizes the start and end of the reporting window.
processingSteps: 1. Diagnose the under-count: the original `created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` treats the upper bound as midnight, dropping all Jan 31 daytime orders.
2. Rewrite to a half-open interval: `created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'`.
3. Verify the index on created_at is used via EXPLAIN, confirming an index range scan.
4. Aggregate with SUM(amount) and GROUP BY date to produce the daily breakdown.
5. Cross-check the corrected total against a COUNT to confirm Jan 31 rows are now included.
endToEndExample.output: A corrected daily revenue table for all 31 days of January, including the full set of January 31 orders that the original BETWEEN query had silently excluded.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Track daily row counts; a sudden dip on the last day of any month flags a recurrence of the BETWEEN midnight trap. Alert if the corrected total diverges from the legacy total by more than a defined threshold.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Validate that the window start is strictly less than the window end before executing; if a NULL bound is passed, fail fast rather than returning a silently empty or partial result.
endToEndExample.finalResult: An accurate January revenue report. The team adopts the half-open `>= AND <` pattern as a standard for all timestamp windows, eliminating the recurring month-end under-count while keeping queries index-friendly.

industryUseCases.problem: Generating sales and order reports scoped to a specific date window and filtering products into price tiers.
industryUseCases.solution: Use BETWEEN for inclusive price bands (`price BETWEEN 10 AND 50`) and half-open `>= AND <` ranges for timestamped order windows to avoid month-end under-counting.
industryUseCases.benefits: Accurate revenue reporting, correct price-bucket segmentation, and index-friendly range scans that keep dashboards fast at scale.

industryUseCases.company: Banking and Financial Services (e.g., Visa, PayPal)
industryUseCases.problem: Auditing transactions within a settlement window and flagging amounts outside approved limits.
industryUseCases.solution: Apply BETWEEN for inclusive amount thresholds (`amount BETWEEN 0 AND 10000`) and NOT BETWEEN to surface out-of-policy transactions for review.
industryUseCases.benefits: Precise compliance reporting, reliable detection of transactions outside permitted ranges, and auditable, deterministic filter logic.

industryUseCases.company: IoT and Monitoring (e.g., Datadog, sensor platforms)
industryUseCases.problem: Querying time-series sensor readings within a window and isolating readings within or outside normal operating ranges.
industryUseCases.solution: Use half-open time-window filters on indexed/partitioned timestamp columns and BETWEEN on numeric reading values to find in-spec measurements.
industryUseCases.benefits: Efficient partition pruning over huge time-series volumes and correct, boundary-safe selection of telemetry data.

productionDeepDive.scalability: BETWEEN scales well when the test column is indexed or the table is partitioned on it, because the engine performs a bounded range scan or prunes partitions; the cost grows with the size of the range, not the table.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: The operator is stateless and deterministic. Resilience hinges on consistent data typing — schema migrations that change a DATE to a TIMESTAMP can quietly introduce the midnight-boundary bug, so regression tests should pin expected row counts.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: BETWEEN executes identically across replicas; read-replica routing of range-scan reports offloads analytical queries from the primary without changing results.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because results depend only on data and bounds, point-in-time restores reproduce identical BETWEEN results; no special handling is needed beyond standard backup integrity.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep the column bare (no functions) so the predicate stays sargable; index the range column; for time-series use partitioning plus half-open windows to maximize partition pruning and minimize bytes scanned.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: In serverless/columnar warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift Spectrum) that bill by data scanned, restricting BETWEEN/half-open windows to partitioned date columns prunes data and cuts query cost substantially.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Bound values frequently come from user input (date pickers, filter forms); always bind them as parameters to prevent SQL injection, and validate that low <= high server-side.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Instrument report row counts and flag boundary anomalies (e.g., last-day dips). Capture and review EXPLAIN plans periodically to confirm range scans rather than full scans.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Reconcile inclusive BETWEEN results against half-open equivalents during testing; mismatches reveal hidden boundary or NULL-handling issues. Assert that no NULL bounds reach production queries.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log the resolved bound values with each report run for auditability, and alert when a query's scanned-bytes or row count deviates sharply from its historical baseline for the same window size.

recommendedPractices: **Use half-open ranges for timestamps:** Prefer `ts >= start AND ts < next_period` over BETWEEN for any column carrying a time component.
**Keep the column bare:** Do not wrap the test column in functions (e.g. avoid `DATE(ts) BETWEEN ...`) so the predicate remains sargable.
**Order bounds low-then-high:** Always write the smaller value first; BETWEEN does not auto-swap reversed bounds.
**Parameterize bounds:** Bind range endpoints as parameters to avoid SQL injection and enable plan reuse.
engineeringStandards: Reserve BETWEEN for inclusive numeric ranges and pure DATE columns; mandate half-open intervals for TIMESTAMP/DATETIME windows in code review.
Ensure the column referenced in a range predicate is indexed (or the partition key) on large tables.
Use explicit type casts on bounds when the column type and literal type differ to avoid implicit conversion.
designRecommendations: Define reporting periods as half-open intervals end-to-end (period start inclusive, next period start exclusive) so adjacent periods tile without gaps or overlaps.
Store true dates as DATE and true instants as TIMESTAMP so the right range pattern is obvious from the type.
Expose date filters in UIs as full-day-inclusive but translate them to half-open SQL behind the scenes.
namingConventions: Name bound parameters clearly, e.g. `:start_date` and `:end_date_exclusive`, signaling inclusive/exclusive intent.
Suffix exclusive upper bounds with `_exclusive` or `_lt` to document the half-open convention.
documentationStandards: Document whether each range filter is inclusive or half-open in the query or report definition.
Note the column's data type (DATE vs TIMESTAMP) next to any range predicate to justify the chosen pattern.
Record the boundary convention (inclusive both ends for BETWEEN) in team SQL style guides.
testingStrategies: Add boundary tests with rows exactly on the low and high bounds to confirm they are included.
Add a row dated on the last day of a window at a non-midnight time to catch the TIMESTAMP BETWEEN trap.
Compare BETWEEN results against the half-open equivalent in CI to detect off-by-one discrepancies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using BETWEEN on a TIMESTAMP column with date-only bounds.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers think of '2024-01-31' as 'all of January 31', but the database interprets it as 2024-01-31 00:00:00.
commonMistakes.impact: Every event on the last day after midnight is silently dropped, under-counting reports — a bug that often goes unnoticed for months.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a half-open interval: `ts >= '2024-01-01' AND ts < '2024-02-01'`, which includes all timestamps of the period regardless of time-of-day.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming BETWEEN automatically sorts the two endpoints.
commonMistakes.impact: The predicate expands to `>= 500 AND <= 100`, which is unsatisfiable, so the query returns zero rows with no error.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always place the lower value first. If bounds are dynamic, validate or sort them (least/greatest) before building the predicate.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting BETWEEN excludes NULLs and assuming NOT BETWEEN includes them.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Misunderstanding three-valued logic; expecting NOT BETWEEN to return 'everything else', including NULLs.
commonMistakes.impact: Rows with NULL in the test column disappear from both BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN results, causing apparent data loss in 'outside the range' reports.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Handle NULLs explicitly, e.g. `col NOT BETWEEN a AND b OR col IS NULL`, when NULL rows must appear in the complement set.

comparisonSection.explanation: They are semantically identical — the parser rewrites BETWEEN into the comparison pair — so performance is the same. BETWEEN is more readable and avoids repeating the column, but cannot express a half-open (exclusive upper) range, which the explicit comparisons can.

BETWEEN's inclusive upper bound plus midnight interpretation silently drops same-day events on TIMESTAMP columns. The half-open form includes every instant of the period and tiles cleanly with adjacent periods, making it the safer choice for time windows.

Both return values strictly outside [a, b] and both exclude NULLs. NOT BETWEEN is more concise; the OR form makes the boundary logic explicit and is easier to extend with an `OR col IS NULL` clause when NULLs must be included.

beginnerQuestions.question: Is the SQL BETWEEN operator inclusive or exclusive?
beginnerQuestions.answer: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. `x BETWEEN 1 AND 10` matches values from 1 to 10, including both 1 and 10. It is equivalent to `x >= 1 AND x <= 10`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers test whether you know the boundary semantics. State clearly that both endpoints are included and give the >= AND <= equivalence.

beginnerQuestions.question: How does NOT BETWEEN behave?
beginnerQuestions.answer: `col NOT BETWEEN a AND b` returns rows where col is strictly less than a OR strictly greater than b. It is the negation of BETWEEN and, like BETWEEN, excludes rows where col is NULL.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show you understand it as `col < a OR col > b` and mention the NULL exclusion to demonstrate depth.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why can `created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'` miss rows on January 31?
intermediateQuestions.answer: If created_at is a TIMESTAMP, the literal '2024-01-31' is interpreted as 2024-01-31 00:00:00. The inclusive upper bound therefore only matches that exact midnight instant, excluding all Jan 31 events later in the day. The fix is a half-open range: `created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'`.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is the single most common BETWEEN interview gotcha. Explain the implicit midnight conversion and give the half-open fix.

intermediateQuestions.question: Is BETWEEN slower than writing two comparisons?
intermediateQuestions.answer: No. The parser rewrites `BETWEEN a AND b` into `>= a AND <= b`, so the optimizer produces the same plan and performance. The choice between them is about readability and the ability to express half-open ranges, not speed.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding that BETWEEN is syntactic sugar. Mention sargability and that both forms use the same index range scan.

advancedQuestions.question: How does BETWEEN interact with indexes and partition pruning on large tables?
advancedQuestions.answer: When the test column is a bare indexed column, BETWEEN is sargable: the optimizer seeks to the lower bound in a B-tree and scans forward to the upper bound, reading only qualifying entries. On partitioned tables, a BETWEEN/half-open filter on the partition key lets the engine prune non-overlapping partitions entirely, so cost scales with range size, not table size. Wrapping the column in a function breaks sargability and forces a full scan.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate the link between predicate form, sargability, index range scans, and partition pruning, and the consequence of non-sargable function-wrapped columns.

advancedQuestions.question: What happens with `BETWEEN high AND low` (reversed bounds), and why does it return no rows?
advancedQuestions.answer: BETWEEN does not reorder its operands. `BETWEEN 500 AND 100` expands to `>= 500 AND <= 100`, which no value can satisfy, so it returns zero rows — silently, with no error. For dynamic bounds, sort them with LEAST/GREATEST before constructing the predicate.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows you understand the literal expansion and the silent-failure risk, plus a defensive mitigation.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A monthly revenue dashboard built on a TIMESTAMP order column reports totals that are consistently a bit low, and the gap is always largest at month-end. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: A month-end-concentrated shortfall points to the last day being truncated. Inspect the filter; a BETWEEN with a date-only upper bound on a TIMESTAMP column truncates the final day to midnight. Confirm by counting rows on the last day. Replace with a half-open interval and re-validate counts.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: The query uses `created_at BETWEEN start AND end` where end is a date interpreted as midnight, excluding same-day-after-midnight orders. Replace it with `created_at >= start AND created_at < next_month_start`. Verify the corrected total now includes all last-day orders and standardize the half-open pattern across reports.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the query layer for a time-series analytics service that must serve fast, correct windowed range queries over billions of rows.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Partition the fact table by day or hour on an indexed timestamp column. Express every window as a half-open `>= window_start AND < window_end` predicate so the engine prunes partitions and uses range scans. Use BETWEEN only for inclusive numeric metric thresholds, not time windows.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Half-open windows guarantee boundary correctness and clean tiling of adjacent periods at the cost of being slightly more verbose than BETWEEN. Finer partitioning improves pruning but increases metadata overhead.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Scale reads with partition pruning plus columnar storage; route heavy analytical range scans to read replicas or a columnar warehouse. Cap query windows server-side and reject reversed or NULL bounds before execution.

How would you detect that a BETWEEN predicate has become non-sargable?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: BETWEEN a AND b filters values in the inclusive range [a, b], exactly equivalent to `>= a AND <= b`.
keyConcepts: NULLs are excluded by BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN.
Use half-open >= AND < for TIMESTAMP windows.
formulas: expr BETWEEN low AND high  <=>  expr >= low AND expr <= high
expr NOT BETWEEN low AND high  <=>  expr < low OR expr > high
commands: SELECT * FROM t WHERE col BETWEEN 100 AND 500;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE col NOT BETWEEN 100 AND 500;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE ts >= '2024-01-01' AND ts < '2024-02-01';
interviewPoints: Inclusive both ends — most common gotcha.
TIMESTAMP + date-only bound drops last day; use half-open.
Reversed bounds return zero rows, no error.
Keep column bare to stay sargable / index-friendly.
quickNotes: BETWEEN does not auto-swap bounds; low must come first.
On TIMESTAMP columns prefer `>= start AND < next_period`.
NULL in value or bound excludes the row from both BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN.
Avoid functions on the column (e.g. DATE(ts) BETWEEN ...) to preserve index usage.

keyTakeaways: BETWEEN is inclusive on both bounds and is exact shorthand for `>= low AND <= high`; there is no exclusive variant.
On TIMESTAMP columns, a date-only upper bound is read as midnight and silently drops same-day events — use a half-open `>= start AND < next_period` window instead.
Reversed bounds (`BETWEEN high AND low`) return zero rows with no error, and NULL values/bounds are excluded by both BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN.
BETWEEN is syntactic sugar with identical performance to the comparison pair; keep the test column bare so the predicate stays sargable for index range scans and partition pruning.
Use BETWEEN for inclusive numeric ranges and pure DATE columns; reach for explicit half-open comparisons whenever the upper bound should be exclusive or the column carries a time component.
